result: The study screened six MP-OSN types using GC-SSR with headspace collections from 52 ecologically relevant odor sources (34 fruits, 7 microbes, 11 mammal feces) containing 11,326 distinguishable FID peaks. Of these, 328 peaks elicited responses, with 225 corresponding to 20 identified compounds from four chemical classes. NMDS analysis showed that MP-OSN responses could categorize the odor sources into three distinct groups (fruits, microbes, feces) with statistical significance (ANOSIM R=0.61, p<0.0001).
evaluation: Claims C21-C38 describe a comprehensive GC-SSR screening approach with clear experimental design, sample sizes, and statistical validation. The NMDS analysis with ANOSIM provides appropriate statistical support for the categorization claim (C33). The identification of compounds via GC-MS and co-injection with standards (C36) follows rigorous analytical chemistry protocols. The data are well-documented in figures and tables.

result: PCA analysis using 32 DRAGON descriptors showed that compounds activating different MP-OSNs distributed widely in odor space, while compounds activating the same MP-OSN clustered together, except for pb2A ligands. The pb2A exception is explained by this neuron expressing two receptors (Or33c and Or85e). PCA including (-)-fenchone (a known Or85e ligand) suggests furaneol methylether is detected by Or33c, while (-)-camphor, alpha-ionone, and beta-ionone are detected by Or85e.
evaluation: Claims C39-C44 present a logical chemometric analysis using established DRAGON descriptors and PCA methodology. The inference about receptor specificity (C43-C44) is reasonable based on the clustering pattern with the known Or85e ligand (-)-fenchone (C42), though this remains an inference rather than direct experimental validation. The approach is sound and the conclusion is appropriately qualified as a suggestion.

result: Each MP-OSN type has one or two best ligands (pb1B and pb3B each have two) and detects these with high sensitivity. Detection thresholds were 10^-7 dilution for pb1A, pb1B, pb2B, and pb3B; 10^-6 for pb2A; and 10^-4 for pb3A. This high sensitivity suggests MP-OSNs could evaluate odor sources over long distances similar to antennae.
evaluation: Claims C4-C49 are supported by dose-response data shown in Figures 2 and 3. The detection thresholds are clearly quantified with error bars indicating replication. The inference about long-range detection (C49) is reasonable given the demonstrated sensitivity levels, though it appropriately remains speculative. The experimental approach using serial dilutions is standard and appropriate.

result: Prior to this study, few or no ligands were identified for MP-OSNs, and previously identified ligands were better ligands for Ant-OSNs. GC-SSR screening of antennal OSNs revealed that four MP-OSN best activators (5-hexen-3-one, methyleugenol, furaneol methylether, phenol) elicited no antennal responses, while four others activated both systems. For three compounds (4-ethylguaiacol, 2-phenethyl acetate, phenethyl propionate), MP-OSNs had detection thresholds two orders of magnitude lower than Ant-OSNs. Only butyl 3-hydroxy butyrate was primarily detected by antenna (ab2B). Thus, MP-OSNs are the sole or primary detectors of seven compounds at ecologically relevant concentrations.
evaluation: Claims C22-C55 are well-supported by comparative GC-SSR data (Figure 4A) and dose-response experiments (Figure 4B,C). The systematic screening of all antennal OSN types provides comprehensive evidence. The statistical comparisons of detection thresholds are appropriate, and the phylogenetic observation about receptor clustering (C52) adds evolutionary context. The conclusion (C55) is appropriately qualified to ecologically relevant concentrations.

result: Six of eight tested MP-OSN best ligands were behaviorally active in D. melanogaster: two in T-maze (5-hexen-3-one, furaneol methylether), four in trap assays (4-ethylguaiacol, methyleugenol, 2-phenethyl acetate, phenethyl propionate), and one in wind tunnel (furaneol methylether). Orco[2] mutants showed no attraction, indicating Or gene requirement. At high concentration (10^-2), three compounds elicited Or-independent repulsion. Thus, MP-OSN ligands represent positive cues at lower concentrations requiring Or genes, while higher concentrations elicit Or-independent responses.
evaluation: Claims C56-C66 are supported by behavioral data in Figure 5A-B and supplementary figures. The use of Orco[2] mutants provides appropriate genetic controls (C60-C61). The concentration-dependent behavioral switch (C62-C66) is well-documented with both WT and mutant flies. Statistical tests (Wilcoxon signed rank, Mann-Whitney U) are appropriate for the data. The conclusion appropriately distinguishes between Or-dependent and Or-independent mechanisms.

result: Surgical ablation experiments showed that for four compounds (4-ethylguaiacol, 5-hexen-3-one, methyleugenol, furaneol methylether), palp amputation abolished attraction while antennal amputation had no effect. For 2-phenethyl acetate and phenethyl propionate, the opposite pattern was observed. Genetic ablation of pb2A OSNs (via Or33c-Gal4 or Or85e-Gal4 driving hid) significantly reduced attraction to furaneol methylether in wind tunnel assays.
evaluation: Claims C67-C71 are supported by surgical ablation data (Figure 5C) and genetic ablation data (Figure 5D). The complementary results from surgical and genetic approaches strengthen the conclusions. The finding that 2-phenethyl acetate and phenethyl propionate require antennae (C69-C70) is consistent with the earlier observation that these compounds also activate antennal OSNs (C51). Statistical comparisons are appropriate (Kruskal-Wallis with Dunn's multiple comparison).

result: The maxillary palp organization, OSN types, sensillum pairing, and detection of D. melanogaster best activators are conserved in D. suzukii. The Or genes are also conserved with high amino acid sequence identity: Or33c (82.2%), Or42a (90%), Or46a (83.5%), Or59c (78.4%), Or71a (81.4%), Or85d (86.5%), and Or85e (85%).
evaluation: Claims C72-C75 are supported by GC-SSR data from D. suzukii (Figure 6A) and sequence analysis. The gene sequences were properly cloned, sequenced, and deposited in public databases (accession numbers provided). The amino acid sequence identities are clearly quantified. The comparative GC-SSR approach directly demonstrates functional conservation of detection (C74). The claim of organizational conservation (C72-C73) is supported by the electrophysiological recordings.

result: In D. suzukii, behavioral responses to yeast-produced 2-phenethyl acetate and phenethyl propionate and the ripening signal furaneol methylether are conserved. However, responses to fermentation signals 4-ethylguaiacol and methyleugenol are not conserved. These behavioral changes might represent taxon-specific adaptation to D. suzukii's ecological niche of ripening (rather than fermenting) fruits.
evaluation: Claims C78, C80, C85-C87 are supported by behavioral data in Figure 6B showing differential responses in D. suzukii compared to D. melanogaster. The interpretation (C88) is appropriately speculative and consistent with the known ecological difference between the species (C89-C91). The parallel to CO2 detection conservation without behavioral conservation (C81) provides supporting context. The conclusion logically connects the behavioral differences to ecological niche differences.

result: D. suzukii is an agricultural pest that recently invaded North America and Europe from Asia, causing economic damage to soft fruit crops. Unlike D. melanogaster, D. suzukii feeds and oviposits on undamaged, ripening fruits. The novel attractants identified could potentially be used in integrated pest management (IPM) programs.
evaluation: Claims C89-C91 are background knowledge supported by citations. However, the IPM application claim (C8) is purely speculative and lacks any experimental validation. No field trials, trap efficacy tests, or pest management experiments are presented. While the identification of attractants is a necessary first step, the claim that these "could potentially be used" in IPM requires substantial additional work including field validation, optimization of delivery systems, and demonstration of practical efficacy. The claim is appropriately qualified as potential but remains unvalidated.

result: D. melanogaster has two peripheral olfactory organs: antenna (with four sensillum types) and maxillary palp (with three basiconic sensillum types, each housing two OSNs). The antenna is involved in finding food, oviposition sites, and mates. Prior work suggested MP-OSNs might function in taste enhancement due to overlapping response spectra with antennal OSNs and proximity to taste organs, but the functional significance remained unknown. Six MP-OSN types express seven olfactory receptors, with Or71a previously shown to detect dietary antioxidant proxies.
evaluation: Claims C1-C20 represent established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations. The anatomical descriptions (C1, C9-C11) are well-established. The prior hypothesis about taste enhancement (C12-C13) is properly attributed to previous work. The statement that functional significance remained unknown (C3) appropriately sets up the knowledge gap addressed by this study. All claims are either direct observations or properly cited prior work.

result: 2-phenethyl acetate and phenethyl propionate are yeast-produced volatiles. Furaneol methylether is a ripening signal. 4-ethylguaiacol and methyleugenol are fermentation signals produced by yeast metabolism of hydrocinnamic acids. A parallel case exists where D. melanogaster CO2 avoidance behavior is not conserved in D. suzukii despite conservation of detection and genes.
evaluation: Claims C76-C77, C79, and C81 are background knowledge properly supported by citations to prior work. These claims provide ecological context for interpreting the behavioral results. The CO2 example (C81) provides a useful parallel case of detection conservation without behavioral conservation, strengthening the interpretation of the fermentation signal results.

result: Contrary to previous assumptions that MP-OSNs have low sensitivity and function in taste enhancement, this study shows MP-OSN sensitivity can be as high as Ant-OSNs. MP-OSN specific ligands attracted walking flies over short distances, and furaneol methylether motivated flies to fly toward the source.
evaluation: Claims C82-C84 represent summary conclusions well-supported by the dose-response data (Figures 2-3) and behavioral experiments (Figure 5). The comparison to prior assumptions (C82) appropriately contextualizes the findings. The distinction between short-range walking attraction (C83) and long-range flight attraction (C84) is supported by the different behavioral assays used (T-maze/trap vs. wind tunnel).
